title: Python for Data Analysis
description: Practise the compact syntax that data code is written in.

lessons.title: Loops in one line
lessons.lead: Read a comprehension as: the expression, for each item, optionally where a condition holds.

tasks.title: Three comprehensions
tasks.brief: Build the passing scores, a curved set of scores, and a lookup of name lengths — each as a single comprehension.
steps: Keep the scores of 50 and above
Curve every score by 5 points, but never above 100
Build `{name: length}` for the three names
starter: # 2. every score curved by 5, capped at 100
tasks.hint: `min(s + 5, 100)` caps a curved score, and `{k: v for ... }` builds a dictionary.
solution: print([s for s in scores if s >= 50])
print({name: len(name) for name in names})
tasks.explain: The `if` clause filters, the expression before `for` transforms. A comprehension can do either, or both at once.

tasks.title: Clean a list of place names
tasks.brief: Strip the stray whitespace and fix the capitalisation, then keep only the two-word names.
steps: `.strip()` removes the spaces, `.title()` fixes the case
Do both inside one comprehension
A name is two words when `len(name.split()) == 2`
tasks.hint: String methods chain: `place.strip().title()` runs left to right.
solution: print([place for place in cleaned if len(place.split()) == 2])
tasks.explain: Naming the intermediate list is worth it here — the second comprehension reads from it instead of repeating the cleaning.

lessons.title: Small anonymous functions
lessons.lead: A lambda is used where a function is expected for a moment and never again — most often as a `key=`.

tasks.title: Rank the students
tasks.brief: Sort the students by score, highest first, and print just their names in that order.
steps: Pass `key=lambda s: s["score"]` to `sorted`
Add `reverse=True` for highest first
Print the names as a list
starter: # sort by score, highest first, then print the names
tasks.hint: `sorted` gives you back whole dictionaries — pull the names out afterwards with a comprehension.
solution: ranked = sorted(students, key=lambda s: s["score"], reverse=True)
tasks.explain: The lambda tells `sorted` what to compare. Without it, Python would try to compare whole dictionaries and raise a TypeError.

tasks.title: Sort by two things at once
tasks.brief: Sort the words by length first, and alphabetically within the same length.
steps: A lambda can return a tuple: `lambda w: (len(w), w)`
Tuples compare left to right, so length wins and the word breaks the tie
tasks.hint: One `sorted` call is enough — the tuple key does both jobs.
tasks.explain: This is the standard way to sort by several fields — build a tuple in the order you want them compared.

lessons.title: Transform, then select
lessons.lead: `map` applies a function to every item; `filter` keeps the items that pass a test. Both are lazy, so wrap them in `list()`.

tasks.title: Fix the types coming out of a CSV
tasks.brief: Convert the raw strings to floats with `map`, then print the list and its average rounded to two places.
steps: `map(float, raw)` needs no lambda — pass the function by name
Wrap the result in `list()` before using it twice
starter: # 2. their average, rounded to two places
tasks.hint: A map object can only be walked once — that is why `list()` matters when you need it twice.
tasks.explain: Every value read from a CSV arrives as a string. Converting on the way in prevents a whole category of bugs later.

tasks.title: Drop the empty values
tasks.brief: Use `filter` twice: once to remove the empty and missing names, once to keep the passing scores.
steps: `filter(None, items)` keeps everything truthy
The scores need a lambda: keep 50 and above
tasks.hint: `filter(None, ...)` is a shortcut — passing `None` as the function means "keep what is truthy".
tasks.explain: `[s for s in scores if s >= 50]` does the same job as the second line, and most Python teams prefer it. Know both — you will read both.

lessons.title: Walk two lists side by side
lessons.lead: zip pairs items by position and stops at the shortest input.

tasks.title: Pair names with scores
tasks.brief: Print one aligned line per student, then build a dictionary from the two lists.
steps: Format each line as `f"{name:<6} {score:>5}"`
`dict(zip(names, scores))` builds the lookup in one step
starter: # 2. the same data as a dictionary
tasks.hint: `for name, score in zip(names, scores):` unpacks each pair straight into two variables.
solution: for name, score in zip(names, scores):
tasks.explain: `:<6` pads a string to six characters on the left, `:>5` pushes a number to the right of five. That is how columns line up without a table.

tasks.title: All four together
tasks.brief: Convert, combine, filter, and sort — the whole toolkit on one small dataset.
steps: Convert the scores to floats with `map`
Build a list of `{"name": …, "score": …}` dictionaries with `zip`
Keep the students who scored 50 or more with `filter`
Sort them by score, highest first, and print the names
tasks.hint: Print the four results in the order the steps list them: the floats, the number of students, the number who passed, then the ranked names.
solution: students = [{"name": n, "score": s} for n, s in zip(names, scores)]
ranked = sorted(passed, key=lambda s: s["score"], reverse=True)
tasks.explain: This is the shape of most small analyses: read, convert, combine, filter, order. Modules 03 and 04 do the same work on whole columns at once.
